title: Day 0 support for Reflection’s Beam on Google Cloud: 5x faster perf with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo
raw_text: Today, Reflection released Beam , its first open-weight model built to give developers, researchers, and enterprises open control and customization for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by solving complex reasoning and coding problems with 3x to 4x higher reasoning compute efficiency than comparable open models. Alongside today’s release, Google Cloud is announcing day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for serving Beam on Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure. To help developers get the full benefit of Beam’s token efficiency in production, we worked with Reflection to optimize performance of the underlying serving stack using llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang) on Google Cloud: "By deploying our Beam model on Google Cloud, we achieved up to 5x higher performance and 8x lower latency to optimize serving of agentic workloads." - Joe Spisak, VP of Product & Head of Open Source, Reflection With today’s day 0 release on Google Cloud, developers get: Compounding model and system efficiency: Combining Beam’s 3x to 4x reasoning compute efficiency with system-level optimizations on A4X Max instances (NVIDIA GB300 NVL72) for up to 5x higher throughput and 8x lower latency,* and G4 VMs (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) for up to 2x higher throughput and 8x lower latency.* High-efficiency multi-turn serving: KV-cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, speculative decoding and hierarchical KV cache offloading to Host DRAM and Local SSD reduce redundant prompt recomputation across long coding sessions. Turnkey optimized deployment: Our recommended performance optimized recipes for agentic workloads with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo are available in AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes , llm-d repo and Model Garden in Gemini platform with a few clicks. *Based on customer benchmarking Scaling inference requires system-level optimization When evaluating models for agentic coding and tool use, inference efficiency happens at two distinct layers: how efficiently the model reasons and how efficiently the serving system executes multi-turn loops . Model-level efficiency: Reflection’s Beam Reflection designed Beam ( ~501B total parameters with ~23B active parameters per token, and an approximately 1M -token context window) specifically for text-native software engineering and multi-step tool use. It plugs directly into the coding harnesses developers already use, including Reflection’s Mirror CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, and , to resolve GitHub issues, run CLI and DevOps workflows, and complete long-horizon tasks. Because Beam activates only 23B parameters per token and reaches solutions using 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens than other comparable open weight models, it dramatically reduces the inference-time compute required for each reasoning step. System-level efficiency: AI Hypercomputer optimized serving Once developers deploy an agent into production, a second set of bottlenecks could appear at the serving layer. In an agentic coding loop, the model is called dozens of times in a single session. With every turn, the coding harness appends new file reads, code diffs, compiler logs, and tool outputs to a shared conversation history that quickly grows to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens. Even when the model itself generates 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens on each turn, the accumulated context window across turns creates two major infrastructure challenges: First, prefill compute becomes a bottleneck . Standard Kubernetes load balancers distribute requests using stateless round-robin routing. When a coding harness sends Turn 15 of a session, it often lands on a different replica than Turn 14. That replica is forced to recompute the entire historical prompt from scratch, wasting GPU compute and creating long prefill queues that delay other users. Second, decode becomes bottlenecked by KV cache capacity . Holding long-context KV caches for dozens of concurrent agent sessions quickly fills up GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, the serving engine has to evict older KV blocks. As soon as those blocks are evicted, cache hit rates drop and GPU throughput stalls. To preserve Beam’s model-level efficiency at cluster scale, the serving stack has to be optimized as a distributed system. That is why our recipes pair Beam with llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang). Inside the AI Hypercomputer inference architecture To run Beam’s BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints at peak efficiency on Day 0, we designed a vertically integrated architecture on AI Hypercomputer where each layer handles a specific part of the agentic serving lifecycle. System optimized architecture for serving agentic traffic Rather than treating inference pods as stateless endpoints, each layer of the stack is co-designed around the multi-turn agent lifecycle: Prefix- and load-aware routing (GKE + llm-d EPP / Dynamo router): Tracks cached prefixes and queue depth across worker pods, steering each follow-up turn from a coding harness to the replica holding its warm KV prefix while preventing queue saturation via turn-priority flow control. Disaggregated compute and speculative decoding (A4X Max & G4 instance) : Runs vLLM and SGLang with native Blackwell NVFP4, Expert Parallelism (EP) for Beam’s 23B active experts, Data-Parallel Attention, and DFlash2 speculative decoding. Separating Prefill and Decode (P/D) pools ensures heavy prompt bursts never stall active token generation. Tiered KV cache (GPU Memory -> DRAM & Local SSD) Active KV blocks stay in high-bandwidth GPU memory ( Tier 1 ), while warm KV blocks evicted during long-horizon sessions overflow into host CPU DRAM and local NVMe SSDs ( Tier 2 ) via vLLM’s OffloadingConnector or SGLang's HiCache, allowing historical context to be fetched in milliseconds instead of recomputed from scratch. System optimizations for multi-turn agentic workloads When serving multi-turn coding and tool-use workloads like the AgentX trajectory dataset across rising concurrency levels, each layer in the serving stack contributes to the performance and latency improvements for multi-turn, long context traffic patterns of agentic workloads: A note on reading these charts. The two configurations are not comparable to each other. NVIDIA Dynamo ran on A4X Max instances with 32 x NVIDIA GB300 NVL72GPUs; llm-d ran on G4 VMs with 8 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Each chart shows the gain over a baseline on the same hardware. More replicas give the router more warm KV caches to hit and more room to split prefill from decode, so the uplift grows with the deployment. Both llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo scale up and down to match the underlying infrastructure. NVIDIA Dynamo optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam llm-d optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam Across both platforms, layering these optimizations shifts the Pareto frontier to deliver higher output throughput and faster per-user interactivity simultaneously: Baseline deployment (Stateless round-robin routing). In a standard Kubernetes deployment without prefix awareness, consecutive turns from the same coding session land on different replicas, forcing constant prefill recomputation on historical context and causing throughput to plateau as concurrency scales. KV-cache-aware & flow control routing. Enabling prefix-aware routing in NVIDIA Dynamo or llm-d’s Sticky EPP with turn-priority flow control keeps multi-turn agent trajectories pinned to the replica holding their warm KV cache, immediately cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency and freeing up GPU compute, resulting in a significant increase in token throughput. Host DRAM and Local SSD (LSSD) KV offloading. Offloading evicted KV blocks from GPU memory into host DRAM and local NVMe SSDs prevents cache thrashing when dozens of long-context coding sessions exceed on-device GPU memory capacity. Disaggregated serving, speculative decoding, and KV pool tuning. Tuning hybrid KV cache memory allocation, enabling speculative decoding, and disaggregating prefill and decode workers isolates token generation from heavy prompt bursts while the draft model multiplies output throughput to keep per-agent token interactivity fast. Get started and meet us at PyTorchCon and GTC Berlin This blog explored how you can leverage system level optimizations to scale performance to serve Reflection's Beam family of models for agentic workloads. All of the Kubernetes manifests, router configurations, and benchmarking scripts from this post are open-source and ready to run on your own GKE cluster. Deploy the optimized stack : Explore the day 0 guides for running Reflection’s Beam with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo in the AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes repository on A4X Max and G4 , and Model Garden in Gemini platform. Download the weights : Grab the Apache 2.0 BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints on Reflection’s Hugging Face page . Visit us at the llm-d and PyTorch Conference in San Jose : If you are attending PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose this October, stop by the llm-d community sessions and the Google Cloud booth #. We will be walking through live demos of KV-cache-aware routing, P/D disaggregation, and KV cache tiering for agentic workloads. Come see us at NVIDIA GTC Berlin: If you are attending NVIDIA GTC Berlin, come connect with us at our booth #3026, or our Google Cloud Hub at w3.hub: just a short 5 minute walk from the venue. Learn more about our sessions .

title: Architecting autonomy: A design pattern for high-compute, governed agents in biotech
raw_text: In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way. Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks. Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech. A three-layer pattern The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery. Figure 1 — The three-layer pattern: a cognitive orchestrator (brain), a scalable GPU execution layer (muscle), and an enterprise governance plane. The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run: Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol . Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM). To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture: Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node. Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference. Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure. This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput. In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody. Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC . The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter. The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime , within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report” , the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below; In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent. Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage . Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down. Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated. By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads. Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts: Common Assumption Architectural Reality Recommended Best Practice "Swap in a faster driver model to cut latency." The primary orchestrator's token generation is rarely the bottleneck in multi-step R&D pipelines. Optimize I/O, not token speed: Focus on reducing payload sizes and intermediate network hops rather than compromising orchestrator reasoning depth. "Parallelize tool calls across workers." External scientific services and containerized models often serialize requests internally on dedicated hardware. Respect execution topology: Align client-side concurrency with backend queue mechanics to prevent pipeline lockouts and connection timeouts. "Pass full simulation states between tools." Large JSON bodies cause schema validation failures, prompt truncation, and token bloat. Pass heavy payloads by reference: Store raw coordinates in object storage and pass lightweight URIs between agent boundaries. "Return outputs only when the pipeline finishes." Long multi-minute runs leave scientists blind to whether jobs are proceeding or stalled. Stream intermediate stage completions: Emit progress updates at each completed milestone (e.g., folding complete , docking running ) for real-time visibility. "Chain multiple granular micro-tools." Deep tool-chains increase the probability of hallucinated arguments and schema mismatches. Collapse compute pipelines: Wrap end-to-end simulation pipelines behind a single, clean tool interface that takes clear parameters and returns a consolidated object. The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: Agent Identity : Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. Agent Gateway : This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. Agent Registry : This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. Model Armor : This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project. In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways; Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher. Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off. The pattern, and the path forward High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways: Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models. Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage. Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight. As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable. Reach out to your Google sales representative if you have any requirements to build a use case like this and we will be happy to talk and support you in your agent development journey on Google Cloud.
summary: In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way.

title: Announcing Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for GKE: Turnkey threat detection for Kubernetes
raw_text:
Everything is moving faster in the age of AI, and that includes security threats. What used to take attackers weeks to exploit can now happen in just a few minutes. Standard vulnerability scans that run on artifacts at rest can catch basic setup issues, but to detect an attack that's actively happening you need real-time runtime protection. Today, we’re introducing the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), in preview. This built-in integration brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's industry-leading eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters. The operational friction of runtime security Security and platform engineering teams share common dilemmas when deploying in-cluster runtime defenses: Deployment and lifecycle friction : Deploying runtime agents often requires managing installations from third-party sources across dozens or hundreds of clusters. Credential sprawl and security risks : Passing and rotating API keys as Kubernetes Secrets introduces administrative overhead and security risk. Fleet-wide enforcement gaps : Platform teams lack built-in policy controls to enforce that every new cluster has runtime sensors enabled before workloads are deployed and start receiving traffic. Performance and operational overhead : Without explicit and strategic resource limits, runtime agents can impact how much CPU and memory is available for your workloads and system functionality. With the Wiz Runtime Sensor for GKE , Google Cloud and Wiz have minimized these operational barriers. The Runtime Sensor is now available in GKE as a first-party, managed platform add-on. Bridging the gap with Wiz Runtime Sensor for GKE The Wiz Runtime Sensor for GKE connects central security and platform engineering workflows by simplifying and automating the sensor lifecycle. Figure 1: High-level architecture showing credential sync, sensor deployment, and threat telemetry. With the add-on, GKE manages the sensor deployment, credential injection, and lifecycle updates. Building runtime protection directly into the platform reduces administrative overhead and provides the following benefits for your Kubernetes fleet: Native Secret Manager integration: Security teams no longer need to distribute Wiz API keys across cluster namespaces. The add-on uses GKE's Secret Manager secret sync integration to store your Wiz credentials in an off-cluster, centralized credential vault that only a dedicated service account can access. GKE automatically retrieves the credentials and injects them directly into the Runtime Sensor pods. Updating a key in Secret Manager automatically syncs to the sensor without requiring cluster restarts or manual intervention. Simplified enablement: After you add your Wiz credentials to Secret Manager, platform operators can enable the Runtime Sensor add-on by using the gcloud CLI or the GKE API. The GKE control plane handles deploying the sensor components, managing the lifecycle of pods, and configuring the nodes. Secure egress and proxy support : For environments that restrict public internet access, the managed sensor supports standard HTTP and mTLS proxy configurations. Telemetry is routed back to Wiz without violating your egress firewall policies. Fleet-wide governance with organization policy : Platform security leads can enforce compliance across their entire organization using custom organization policy constraints . You can use a constraint to reject any attempts to create a cluster that doesn't enable the Runtime Sensor add-on, which can prevent malicious actors from spinning up rogue infrastructure to evade runtime detection. Kernel-level observability with minimal overhead : The Wiz Runtime Sensor continuously monitors system calls, running processes, network connections, and file access. It catches suspicious activity, including reverse shells, unauthorized privilege escalations, container escapes, and unsafe outbound connections while keeping CPU usage low even under heavy workload activity. The sensor uses a fixed memory limit on each node to ensure consistent performance as workload density changes. This is especially valuable for AI workloads and web services where application activity might fluctuate quickly. Independent auto-updates : Security threats and zero-day vulnerabilities don’t wait for scheduled infrastructure maintenance windows. The lifecycle of the Wiz sensor add-on for GKE is independent of your GKE cluster and node lifecycle. The sensor periodically rolls out updates of new sensor versions published by Wiz, to help ensure that your clusters always have the latest detection rules without requiring GKE version bumps, node pool recreations, or workload disruption. How it works: Deploying and enforcing the sensor Enabling the Wiz sensor add-on follows the same process that platform administrators are already familiar with on GKE. Using standard gcloud commands, you can activate runtime protection during cluster creation, turn it on for existing clusters, and enforce it across your fleet while keeping credentials securely managed in Secret Manager. Check the setup documentation for prerequisites, such as granting GKE access to Secret Manager. Provisioning a cluster with the Wiz Sensor add-on To provision a new GKE cluster with the managed Wiz sensor enabled using credentials stored in Secret Manager: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud container clusters create production-ai-cluster \
 --zone=us-central1-a \

 --enable-secret-sync-rotation \
 --addons=WizSensor=ENABLED \
 --wiz-sensor-registry-secret-uri=projects/${PROJECT_ID}/secrets/wiz-registry-secret/versions/latest \

 --update-addons=WizSensor=ENABLED \
 --wiz-sensor-registry-secret-uri=projects/${PROJECT_ID}/secrets/wiz-registry-secret/versions/latest \
 --wiz-sensor-api-key-secret-uri=projects/${PROJECT_ID}/secrets/wiz-api-key-secret/versions/latest'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd61b844490>)])]> Enforcing fleet-wide protection with organization policy You can require all new GKE clusters across your organization to install the runtime sensor by deploying a custom constraint : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'name: organizations/123456789012/customConstraints/custom.GKEWizSensorEnforced

By feeding GKE runtime telemetry into the Wiz Security Graph, you unlock a security toolkit that goes beyond static alerting, with: Real-time risk assessment and threat verification : By pairing background security scans with live activity monitoring, you get a clear view of real risks. The sensor checks whether vulnerable code is actually running in memory, so you can focus on active security threats and ignore inactive ones. Real-time threat detection and response : Identify suspicious activity like malware, unauthorized access attempts, and software vulnerabilities in real time. Security teams can set rules to automatically block or stop threats before they can spread. Network activity and detailed security insights : Track system activity, network connections, and data flows to uncover hidden risks and unauthorized software usage. If a threat is detected, the sensor automatically gathers diagnostic data to help teams quickly investigate what happened. Together, these capabilities ensure that mission-critical applications and AI agents deployed on GKE are monitored for attacks and data exfiltration without compromising developer velocity. title: Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins
raw_text: The real challenge of building an agentic system isn't the construction, it's the measurement. Evaluation engineering is a critical foundation for building reliable AI systems. Setting up systematic, repeatable tests to measure your agent’s true behavior can be the difference between shipping a tool you can trust and one that silently breaks, fails to call APIs, or makes mistakes. I’ve run evaluation engineering initiatives for years at Google and d eveloping the newly released Google Cloud Developer plugin served as a live testbed to stress-test these key principles across real-world developer workflows. Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds. 1. Grade the execution steps instead of the summary When we first evaluated agents, we set up an LLM-as-judge to inspect the agent’s final text reply and scored it against a checklist. However, we quickly realized it’s fundamentally flawed because the grader only sees what the agent wrote, not what it actually did. When we ran our initial 11-prompt evaluation suite for the Google Cloud Developer plugin, the automated grader marked it as failing three prompts. But when we opened the raw tool-call logs and read the transcripts, the plugin had actually passed all three. On a Cloud Run cleanup prompt, for instance, our rubric required checking command syntax before running anything. The agent ran gcloud help run services list as its very first step. It did the work, but its final message was focused on warning the user about permanent data loss rather than reciting that it had checked the help docs. The grader penalized the agent for doing the right thing simply because it didn’t brag about it in the summary. If your rubric line says "did it run X?", a LLM judge is guessing unless you evaluate the actual tool-call trajectory. Takeaway : Don't grade an agent on its closing pitch. Score the raw execution trajectory to verify what commands were actually executed, validated, and scoped. 2. Design evals for asynchronous operations When you start reading tool-call trajectories, how you extract that telemetry matters just as much as what you're reading. Extracting agent telemetry into a flattened, sequential list of events obscures concurrent tool dispatch, which is one of the critical causes of behavioral failure. Modern agent harnesses often batch multiple tool invocations into a single assistant turn using an array of calls. In our evaluations, when an agent was asked to inspect an environment and look up documentation, the harness dispatched the skill-loading call and two documentation searches simultaneously within a single tool_calls payload. Because activating a skill is a multi-stage process, where the initial call returns a short launch stub and the subsequent turn injects the full instruction body, the instructions meant to govern the search arrived in the prompt context after the system had already executed the searches. The system never gave the skill a dedicated turn to let its guidance influence the agent's actions. If telemetry pipelines strip out turn structures and merge calls into a flat timeline, engineers will waste days wondering why an agent disregarded unambiguous instructions that a developer embedded in a skill. Takeaway : Preserve turn structure in telemetry extractors so you can identify when client-side parallel dispatch issues tool calls before injected guidance enters the context window. 3. Test live runs and "dry runs" side-by-side You need to inspect real API calls to catch harness quirks, like parallel dispatch. But if you only test your agent in one environment condition, you're flying half-blind. From day one, you need to run two conditions side-by-side: a live run and a plan-only run. In the live condition, the agent has real, sandboxed credentials and actually executes commands. This is how you see if syntax works, parameters serialize cleanly, and the agent exercises restraint before doing something destructive. Live runs frequently hit an unexpected permission error on step two and abort before you ever reach the behavior you’re trying to test. That's why you need the plan-only condition, where you strip credentials and tell the agent to explain what it would do without running anything. This strips out permission roadblocks and shows you the model’s pure reasoning and routing intent. Roughly half our most important findings came from the delta between the two. For example, on one of our onboarding prompts, a live run was blocked immediately on a project list call. The plan-only run sailed right through and produced an 8,000-character plan that completely ignored organization policies, admin approvals, and governance. The live run masked a major cognitive flaw that the plan-only run exposed in seconds. Takeaway : Run live and plan-only evaluations side by side. Live runs test actual execution and safety restraint; plan-only runs expose the model's raw reasoning and routing without getting tripped up by permission errors. 4. Use “golden sets” as durable baselines Frontier model architectures change every few months, agent harnesses improve, and plugin manifest standards will inevitably evolve. When building the Google Cloud Developer plugin, we treated evaluations as continuous integration testing for these non-deterministic environments. That means we stress-tested the composite stack, including the harness, the live model, and the tools running together on realistic tasks. Instead of guessing from the final text output, this approach captures the whole trajectory: what the agent thought, what commands it actually ran, and whether it solved the problem without breaking anything. Then you score that run against golden sets curated by real human experts who know what the ideal path looks like. Takeaway : Build golden sets based on what the entire system should actually do in the wild, including your harness, model, and plugins. Models change, but those baseline runs are your safety net. Reminder: Use evaluation suites over “one-shot” demos A common mistake I see among engineers is what I like to call the one-shot demo. This is when someone feeds a prompt into a LLM, watches it build a complete 3D game or solves a Rubik’s cube in a single pass and calls it an eval. But in reality, this is just a vanity metric. To do quality work with AI, I truly believe that you need evaluation suites. Without evaluations, teams are like literally running into a dark cave blind. Engineering an enterprise-grade agent means testing the system's ability to handle multi-step interactions, manage permissions, and avoid destructive outcomes like accidentally deleting a project because you asked it to "find opportunities to save costs." Where to go from here Building an agent plugin or MCP server is the beginning. Shipping something you can actually trust with real cloud infrastructure requires significantly more work in evaluations to ensure it’s doing what you expect it to do. At the end of the day, the only thing that outlasts model churn is a stress-tested eval suite. Check out the Google Cloud Developer plugin documentation or explore this codelab to get started with the plugin in Antigravity.

title: The SAVE method: Learn the fundamentals to engineer trustworthy generative media
raw_text: Google Cloud Consulting works with organizations every day to build generative media that’s trustworthy, brand-aligned, and stands out. Instead of relying on clever or complicated prompting, we’ve identified four recurring basics to generate consistent results, what we call the “SAVE” method. In this blog, we’ll share more about this method and how you can apply it to your own work. S - Separate the researcher from the storyteller If in a single prompt, if you’re requesting a technical summary, key product features, and an engaging video script all at once, you’re setting the model up to fail. Creative tasks require fluid language and pacing, while factual output requires constraint. Forcing both jobs into one context window will likely end with the model fabricating details to make the narrative flow better. Instead of one prompt, consider splitting the work into specialized steps, like a researcher and a storyteller. Here’s how they might work together: The researcher reads the source documents, extracts core claims, aligns with approved messaging, and outputs a structured brief (like a clean checklist or bulleted factsheet). The storyteller then takes that verified brief and focuses purely on style, pacing, visual metaphors, and tone. By decoupling research from your creative generation, your agent is never tasked with deciding what’s true, but how to make the truth more engaging and effective. A - Approve verified facts only If you hand a creative generative model documents that are unedited, it might mix up speculative ideas with business facts. The media generator should never have direct access to raw source files. It should only use verified, structured inputs. To avoid this: Lock down core claims : Approved statements, product names, and concrete business outcomes should be fixed upstream rather than left for the model to extract on the spot. Champion contextual packaging : Pass each fact along with its explicit constraints included. Examples may include things like "use this point in the opening statement" or "do not extrapolate beyond this approved bullet point." This way, you ground the generation in verified facts and reduce the risk of unsupported claims entering the creative generation stage. V - Verify before you render Discovering a factual error in an animated video or rendered asset after the final export wastes both compute budget and turnaround time. The most effective human-in-the-loop checkpoint is right before generation begins. To fix this, review the script and storyboard. Have product leads or legal teams sign off on the extracted facts, narrative outline, and voiceover text while it’s still simple, editable text. This way, you can catch errors early. Swapping an outdated feature name or fixing a typo takes two seconds in a text file. Treat text as your testing ground. Once approved, generating the final media becomes a low-risk, predictable step. E - Engineer guardrails into the system Telling a model to “keep voiceover word count short, never reference unapproved topics, and format links correctly" in a prompt works until it doesn’t, and an edge case slips through. Relying on prompt obedience for brand safety is a gamble and can damage trust. Where requirements can be checked deterministically, enforce them in the system rather than relying only on prompt instructions. For example, try these three actions first: Programmatic boundary checks : Use standard code to validate word counts, verify that URLs are live and authorized, check colors against your brand palette, and format text strings. Independent safety gates : Run automated filters outside the generation pipeline to catch policy violations or out-of-bounds claims before an asset is ever delivered. Model modularity : When your safety and brand rules are set, you don't have to rewrite your entire governance playbook every time a newer, faster generative model is launched. You simply plug the new model into your existing, verified pipeline. Generating studio-quality media shouldn't mean constantly worrying about what the model might fabricate next. The SAVE method shifts the burden of accuracy away from prompt phrasing and into the architecture where it belongs. Explore Google Cloud’s generative media suite , featuring cutting-edge models for studio-grade image, video, and sound generation.

title: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run: Scale workers ahead of demand
raw_text: The open-source Temporal execution platform is rapidly becoming a foundational layer of modern software infrastructure — especially for orchestration in distributed systems and AI agent workloads. However, deploying and scaling workers in Temporal comes with unique challenges. Workers poll for tasks instead of serving requests, so request-driven serverless platforms can be an awkward fit. This often results in running worker fleets on Kubernetes or VMs, which you have to manage and pay for continuously. You build a metrics pipeline and tune autoscaling triggers, and scaling still trails bursts because of metrics lag. Every deployment means juggling upgrades and versions, and you pay for that compute whether or not there's work in the queue. We built Cloud Run worker pools for exactly this kind of pull-based work: Your instances connect to a queue or stream, take the next item, and process it. Starting today, Temporal Cloud , which is the fully managed version of Temporal’s open-source platform, can scale them for you. Currently in preview, Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run let you deploy your workers as a worker pool, and Temporal sizes the pool to match the work on your task queues. When there's no work, it can scale the pool to zero. There's no cluster or autoscaler to run, and your worker code stays the same. How Cloud Run worker pools fit with Temporal A worker pool is Cloud Run's resource for continuous background work. It has no public endpoint, and each instance is allocated CPU for its whole lifetime, which matches how a Temporal worker runs. Temporal manages your Cloud Run worker pools as follows: Your Temporal workers run as Cloud Run worker pool instances in your project and poll Temporal Cloud for tasks. Temporal Cloud tracks your task queues and sets the worker pool's instance count through the Cloud Run Admin API, using the IAM permissions you grant. Temporal never opens a connection to your instances, so you don't need to open ports or add firewall rules for it. You run each build version as its own Cloud Run worker pool. An older build's worker pool can sit at zero instances until a workflow that started on it needs it again. Your Temporal workers run in your project, under your service account, and on your network. Temporal decides how many of them run. What you can build with Temporal Serverless Workers The combination of Cloud Run worker pools with Temporal Serverless Workers opens up a variety of interesting use cases: Autoscaled agentic workers: AI agents run multi-step chains of LLM reasoning and tool calls. Temporal's durable execution and Cloud Run worker pools work together here. Temporal workers spin up instantly to handle bursts of LLM steps, embeddings or API calls, then scale to zero when the queue empties. Workers get keyless access to Google Cloud AI APIs. You can also attach a GPU for inference, and the workers attached to the GPUs will still scale to zero. Temporal runs each model and tool call as a durable activity; if a worker disappears mid-step, the activity retries on another worker and the workflow continues. Long-running Workflows : Temporal Workflows can run indefinitely, allowing for building applications that track the state of real-world resources over long periods of time. This pattern is typically known as the “ Entity Pattern ,” because the Workflow represents the state of some entity. However, these long-running Workflows don’t usually have consistent compute requirements: Some individual steps are short, some are long, and other times, the Workflow is sleeping, waiting for external input, such as from a human or another system. Cloud Run worker pools provide flexible compute to support this pattern: Individual steps can run for as long as is required, and Temporal will automatically scale down the worker pool when there is no work to be done. Bursty batch work: Worker pools bill only while instances run, so a worker pool that sits idle between batch runs costs nothing while it's at zero instances. For jobs like billing runs or media transcoding, Temporal scales the pool out as batches arrive and back in once the queue drains. Your maximum instance count caps how many instances you pay for. Tasks beyond that capacity wait in the queue rather than being dropped. Why Cloud Run worker pools for Temporal workers Before, running Temporal workers on Cloud Run services took some workarounds: an HTTP listener, because services expect containers to listen on a port instance-based billing, so workers kept their CPU between requests minimum instances, so the service didn't scale to zero By running Temporal workers on Cloud Run worker pools, you don’t need those workarounds anymore, and you have: No endpoint to manage. There's no public URL or load balancer to lock down, and no health-check port to implement. Steady CPU at a lower price. Instances don't idle or throttle. Cloud Run doesn't remove instances because they look idle, so Temporal alone decides when the pool shrinks. Worker pools list at almost 40% less per vCPU-hour and GB-hour than instance-billed Cloud Run services. Scaling without revision churn. Changing the instance count doesn't create a new revision, so Temporal can resize the pool as often as the load changes. How Temporal manages scaling and versioning of worker pools Temporal decides when to add capacity using one main signal: the delay between a task landing in the task queue backlog and a worker picking it up. If that delay grows, the available workers are saturated. Scaling occurs as follows: Server-side detection: The Temporal server tracks this backlog-to-worker latency for each task queue. Push notification: When the latency crosses its trigger conditions, the server sends a push notification to the worker controller instance. Provisioning: The worker controller then adds capacity to the worker pool. New instances take time to start and connect before they can poll for tasks, so capacity lags behind the signal. Because Temporal keeps spare capacity, the pool grows ahead of demand instead of after tasks pile up. Scale-in is more conservative. Temporal waits for a stabilization period after the last time a task found no available worker (90 seconds by default), and it pauses between successive reductions. Cloud Run’s configurable graceful shutdown extends shutdown from 10 seconds to 10 minutes. That gives SIGTERM-aware workers time to finish or checkpoint. The instance count stays between a minimum and a maximum that you set. If the first task after an idle period can't wait for an instance to start, set the minimum above zero. Deploying new workflow code without breaking running executions is hard. Temporal workflows are stateful and deterministic, so if you swap their code mid-run, you get non-determinism errors. Serverless Workers on Cloud Run solve this by requiring Temporal Worker Versioning. You don't patch code with conditional branches. Instead, you deploy each Worker Deployment Version as its own worker pool deployment, identified by a deploymentName and a buildId . Using distinct worker pools solves two problems: Workflows that started on a particular Worker Deployment Version continue to run and complete on that version. Each Worker Deployment Version is scaled and drained individually, matching compute spend and utilization to the requirements of your application. As existing workflows complete and drain on a previous Worker Deployment Version, the underlying Worker Pool is eventually scaled down to zero automatically. You set a versioning behavior for each Workflow type, or set a Worker-level default: PINNED: A workflow stays on the Worker version (Build ID) it started on and finishes there. Best for short-running workflows, order processing and multi-step APIs. AUTO_UPGRADE: A workflow moves to the new "Current" or "Target" Worker Deployment Version as you roll it out. Best for long-running workflows, such as subscription billing or tasks that run for weeks. Learn more about configuring worker versioning here . Get started Setup takes three steps: Containerize your Temporal Worker and deploy the container as a Cloud Run worker pool, with the Build ID in the pool name. Keep credentials such as your Temporal API key in Secret Manager. Connect Temporal to your worker pool by granting Temporal Cloud permission to manage the worker pool so it can scale it. Create a Worker Deployment Version in Temporal that points at the pool's project, region, and name. Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run is in preview, so APIs and configuration may change before the stable release. To get started, Learn how Serverless Workers on Cloud Run scale and handle versions. Deploy your first worker with the setup guide . See Cloud Run worker pools for CPU, memory, GPU and networking options. Sign up for the configurable graceful shutdown preview .

title: What the Gemini agent means for startups
raw_text: Small teams, short runway, and constant pressure to ship faster — it’s the reality we see every day among the founders we work with at Google for Startups. When you are building a company from the ground up, every hour spent on operational overhead or infrastructure plumbing is an hour taken away from your core product. Last week at Gemini at Work 2026, we introduced the Gemini agent : a single, universal agent designed to work both as your personal assistant and as a dedicated member of your team. And this week, we made our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon , widely available — trained to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks. Here is a look at how the Gemini agent works, five practical takeaways for founders, and how startups are already using it to punch above their weight. What is the Gemini agent? Instead of prompting separate chatbots for writing, coding, and data analysis, the Gemini agent is a single agent that takes high-level objectives and returns finished work. Three principles define it: Unified: A single agent can now handle knowledge work, data analysis, creative asset generation, and writing and running code. For complex jobs, it dynamically spins up temporary, job-specific sub-agents and coordinates their work in parallel or in sequence. Omnipresent access: It works across the surfaces you use every day — on the web, command line, desktop, and mobile, as well as natively inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Chat, and Calendar. Persistent: It runs in the cloud with continuous memory across four dimensions (session, semantic, procedural, and episodic). It onboards itself like a new hire — learning your team, tools, and business context so you don't have to re-explain your startup with every prompt, and keeping multi-day tasks moving even after you close your laptop. For founders wearing five hats at once, Gemini works like a digital chief of staff that's already briefed on your calendar, projects and documents. Ask it to research market trends, build a financial model in Sheets and turn both into a pitch deck, without repeating what the project or goals are at each step. It also works ahead of you. When an investor emails asking for your latest product update as a deck, Gemini spots the request and offers to handle it; one click and it comes back with completed work, ready for sharing or review. Five takeaways for startups 1. Coworker agents and skills help you scale your output Beyond personal assistance, you can create persistent coworker agents that work with your entire team. Each agent comes with its own Workspace account, email address, Drive storage, and directory presence. You can define a specific role — such as a launch coordinator, QA triager, or financial analyst — and your teammates can add agents to a Chat space or @mention it in a Google Doc comment to delegate work. You can also equip agents with reusable skills — or let Gemini write skills for itself as it learns your processes. For example, with operational reporting skills connected to BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog, anyone on your team can ask a plain-language question to build and save a live report. Once saved, those reports run on demand without incurring additional token costs. Gemini also offers pre-built specializations, starting with legal and financial services. What it means for startups: Coworker agents can immediately increase the capacity of your teams, and skills can standardize repeatable processes like investor and operational reporting without burning tokens on every run. 2. Open and third-party model choice Gemini is the agent, and the model underneath is your choice. As startup architectures mature, sending every task to a single frontier model quickly eats into gross margins. With the Gemini agent, you can dynamically route workloads across Gemini models, third-party models like Anthropic’s Claude, and lightweight open models like Gemma . What it means for startups: You get flexibility without lock-in. You can optimize your cost per task — using compact models for high-volume, deterministic jobs and frontier models for complex reasoning — and swap models as your product evolves without rebuilding your workflows. 3. Connected to your services and tools An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. In addition to Google Workspace, the Gemini agent connects directly to your engineering, data, and business stack, including partner solutions: Development and collaboration: Git, Slack, Jira and more Data and local files: BigQuery, Postgres, Snowflake, Databricks, and more alongside files on your desktop Custom tools via MCP: Any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside your network so your engineers can build and share internal tools. What it means for startups: Instead of spending engineering cycles maintaining custom connectors, your team can plug the agent straight into your existing codebase, databases, and MCP tools so it can act on live data wherever it lives. 4. Built-in security and governance For B2B startups, the enterprise security audit is often where deals stall. Under the hood, every agent is assigned a cryptographic Agent Identity for clear audit trails, runs inside an isolated sandbox, and protected with built-in prompt injection defenses. External traffic is routed through Agent Gateway , allowing you to enforce governance policies. And managing coworker agents is as straightforward as managing users today, since they all have a Workspace account. What it means for startups: When an enterprise buyer’s CISO asks how your AI workflows handle data privacy, prompt injection, and access control, you have an enterprise-grade architecture ready — helping you clear procurement hurdles. 5. Protect your runway with real-time cost controls Autonomous agents that run sub-agents for hours or days can quickly run up a bill if a loop goes unchecked. You can now set hard, real-time spend caps directly in the Cloud Billing Console; if a cap is reached, the project's agent automatically pauses so a bug never turns into a billing surprise. Underneath, Gemini runs on Google’s specialized AI infrastructure, including our inference-optimized TPU 8i, which delivers 80% better performance-per-dollar than the prior generation. What it means for startups: You and your developers can experiment with long-running, parallel agentic loops with a built-in financial safety net that protects your cash reserves and builds confidence with your backers. Founders already building Startups and AI-native innovators are already putting Gemini to work. Immersive storytelling platform Whenere used Dreamlands , an agentic 3D worldbuilding platform built on Gemini platform, to bring Pride and Prejudice to Fortnite — with Gemini generating textures for each new object in about 7 seconds for under 10 cents; one artist created nearly 250 custom assets in a single day and completed a historically accurate estate in under a week. They join application-building platform Lovable and fellow startups and innovators including OpenEvidence , Recursion , and Replit and more . Build with Google for Startups The agentic era gives lean teams the leverage to punch far above their weight — whether you’re deploying coworker agents to cover internal operations or building agentic workflows directly into your product. While these new Gemini agent capabilities are not publicly available yet, startups can contact our sales team to learn more and discuss how to get ready. In the meantime, you can explore the Google for Startups program to access credits, hands-on technical guidance, mentorship, global founder community programs and more.

title: What’s new with Google Data Cloud
raw_text: October 12 - October 16 Looker Data Apps are now in Preview to build and host interactive, agent-generated applications natively inside Looker Generated using natural language prompts, the Antigravity CLI, or Claude Code, these interactive web applications, natively hosted inside Looker, transform business reporting into operational systems of action. Users can test scenarios, adjust parameters, and trigger workflows in downstream platforms while inheriting LookML semantic modeling, row-level security, and access controls with no runtime LLM token costs. Read the announcement blog . Build end-to-end data science pipelines with the Data Agent Kit Following the general availability of the Data Agent Kit , a new end-to-end walkthrough demonstrates how data teams can build, test, and schedule machine learning pipelines directly from their preferred code editors. Explore the walkthrough and codelab . Manage dashboard agents as code to bring CI/CD and version control to LookML dashboards Data teams can now declare agent parameters, configurations, and prompt instructions alongside dashboard files in code. This integration enables standard developer workflows for conversational BI, including Git version control, peer review, branching, and automated CI/CD validation before agent modifications reach production end users. Read the technical guide on the Google Developer Community . Simplify AI search with native AlloyDB hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion AlloyDB for PostgreSQL simplifies hybrid search architectures by combining vector similarity search and keyword BM25 retrieval within a unified database engine. Using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), developers can merge lexical scoring and semantic embeddings into a single ranked result without writing a complex SQL query. This unified approach removes the operational overhead of running and synchronizing external search engines alongside operational databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and search applications. Explore hybrid search in AlloyDB . October 5 - October 9 Data Agent Kit is now generally available to bring Google Data Cloud to any coding agent Data Agent Kit provides a free collection of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and Google-authored agent skills that connect more than 15 Google Data Cloud services directly to coding agents across VS Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. This release expands support for developers and data practitioners to inspect schemas, author queries, and build end-to-end data pipelines in natural language directly from their IDE or CLI. Read the announcement blog . Spanner Omni is now generally available for deploy-anywhere, multi-model workloads Spanner Omni brings Spanner's distributed SQL, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities to any environment, including on-premises data centers, other public clouds via Kubernetes or VMs, and local developer laptops. Organizations can build and run multi-model applications with consistent APIs and query engines across hybrid and multi-cloud footprints while seamlessly scaling to managed Spanner on Google Cloud. Read the launch blog and explore how Spanner also removed cumulative mutation limits for DML transactions . AlloyDB delivers PostgreSQL for agents and native BM25 hybrid search We announced PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB , introducing an agentic database architecture engineered for real-time data access at agent scale with workload isolation. In addition, native BM25 ranking is now in Preview for AlloyDB and Cloud SQL , allowing developers to combine keyword search and vector embeddings directly in PostgreSQL without maintaining an external search engine. For hybrid deployments, the AlloyDB Omni RPM Orchestrator is now generally available , and you can dive deeper in our new Build AI apps and agents with AlloyDB eBook . Lakehouse runtime catalog adds regional endpoints across 22 regions and GA support for flexible column names Lakehouse runtime catalog regional endpoints are now live across 22 Google Cloud regions across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East, supporting both the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint and the Apache Hive catalog endpoint to help customers meet strict data residency and sovereignty requirements. title: Bringing the borderless Lakehouse into the agentic era with innovations for Gemini
raw_text: As enterprises shift their AI usage from experimental chatbots to autonomous agents, teams are hitting a critical bottleneck: accessing and reasoning over data scattered across multiple clouds, SaaS platforms, and on-premises systems. To turn AI agents into true systems of action, organizations need a foundation that can handle petabyte-scale reasoning without the security risks of data movement. Last week at our Gemini at Work event, we announced how Gemini can help you transform business workflows. To help power your agents with your enterprise data, we will dive deeper into the new Gemini integration with borderless Lakehouse to help you build, secure, and scale agents that work across your data estate. Access data that lives outside of Google Cloud through Gemini The ultimate value of the borderless Lakehouse is realized through the agents you build to transform your organization, with Gemini as the front door. With the new Gemini integration, data that’s either preconfigured or stored in your borderless Lakehouse is now directly integrated into Gemini. Currently in preview, this means you can set up access to new data sources, such as Databricks Unity Catalog or Snowflake Horizon, through Lakehouse catalog federation directly from Gemini. Now your business users can use natural language to query records that live across clouds while your AI agents can ground their reasoning and generate code from the same data — all without moving it. By directly contextualizing AI agents across your borderless Lakehouse, you can help accelerate your organization’s AI adoption while simplifying access to critical information. Gemini agents invoked by business users can access data that lives in BigQuery and Databricks Unity Catalog to provide comprehensive reporting and get insights using natural language. Borderless Lakehouse advancements In addition to this new, native integration with Gemini, we’re sharing that several features we introduced earlier this year to power your data foundation with the borderless Lakehouse are now generally available, including: Support for Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching for AWS and Azure BigQuery support for Apache Iceberg V3 specifications Read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark Bi-directional caching with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog using Lakehouse runtime federation Integration with Knowledge Catalog Zero-copy data integration with Salesforce, SAP and Workday, and now, Confluent Tableflow Synchronization of Databricks Delta Lake assets through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow Let’s explore. Performance and reasoning at petabyte scale While agent context windows are typically limited to ingesting hundreds of kilobytes at a time, enterprise workflows sometimes join petabytes of data across clouds. An agent-native data platform that needs to combine data across sources, like product and customer data, to your CRM cloud and warehouse telemetry needs to be able to process data at scale. When you do this over MCP, you are limited to megabyte scale because of context windows and payload size. By integrating at every layer of the data and AI stack, the borderless Lakehouse provides enterprise-grade scalability, enabling agents to reason over petabytes of data with similar performance to it being stored locally. At the networking layer, Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching provide high-throughput, low-latency paths to AWS and Azure, eliminating variable egress fees. When an agent joins Iceberg tables in Amazon Azure Data Lake Storage with data in BigQuery, every uncached byte it scans crosses a cloud boundary, so the network sets the pace. Cross-Cloud Interconnect gives the Lakehouse a dedicated, private connection between Google Cloud and AWS or Azure, at 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps per connection. Lakehouse queries travel over that connection rather than the public internet, so latency stays low and predictable. Cross-cloud caching serves repeat reads from inside Google Cloud, so agents can query data in other clouds without migrating it. The borderless Lakehouse includes several key optimizations to integrate Iceberg metadata within the query engine. BigQuery now supports Apache Iceberg V3 specifications, including binary deletion vectors and sort orders. These features allow the engine to handle row-level updates and deletes more efficiently by eliminating the need to rewrite entire data files. We also upgraded BigQuery’s execution engine with a new FlatBuffers-based Parquet reader and parallelized I/O to help reduce CPU overhead and serialization bottlenecks and narrow the performance gap between open formats and native storage. This builds upon recent performance innovations to the query engine designed to support agent workloads, which often come in herds and need to process small queries quickly and cost effectively. With BigQuery fluid scaling and history based optimizations , you can run scalable and efficient agent workloads while maintaining openness with Apache Iceberg. Meanwhile, read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark makes it easy for all of your data teams to work off the same Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage. This vertically optimized stack helps make your agents faster and more cost-effective, leveraging the power of BigQuery and Lightning Engine to activate data without moving it. To expand the analytical depth of the lakehouse, graph support for Iceberg in BigQuery lets you analyze relationship networks, such as supply chains, directly on open table datasets. Comprehensive context and data access for your agents An AI agent is only as smart as the context it can access. To help prevent hallucinations and improve accuracy at the metadata layer, the borderless Lakehouse unifies your enterprise data using the Lakehouse runtime catalog . Based on the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog, it provides bi-directional catalog federation with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog. The Lakehouse runtime catalog also includes a new standard Hive Metastore-compatible endpoint, allowing engines like Apache Spark, Trino, and Presto to discover metadata without architectural changes. The borderless Lakehouse also integrates directly with Knowledge Catalog , which automatically indexes your distributed data assets, to provide the precise business metadata and semantic definitions agents need to reason over your entire enterprise corpus — including unstructured data in Cloud Storage. This gives agents just enough context to be accurate while controlling token costs, helping you develop an intelligent and sustainable agentic strategy. The borderless Lakehouse provides zero-copy data integration with your SaaS applications like Salesforce, SAP and Workday and integrates with a larger partner ecosystem, capturing enterprise data in Knowledge Catalog and acting as a single context engine for your agents. Today, we’re expanding the partner ecosystem with new integrations for Confluent Tableflow, now generally available, which syncs to Lakehouse runtime catalog so the Iceberg tables it produces show up directly in BigQuery, with no copying and no extra ETL. Finally, organizations with Databricks-centric repositories can now easily import, transform and synchronize their Delta Lake assets into Lakehouse through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow. Modernize with ease Customer use of Apache Iceberg has more than tripled since the beginning of 2025, and enterprises building with Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse are seeing significant impact from it: Etsy unified three petabytes with borderless Lakehouse, joining data in place to accelerate pipeline queries by 60%. Commerzbank transforms raw distributed data into governed, agent-ready access. Hightouch integrates directly with borderless Lakehouse so teams can power their marketing directly on an open Iceberg lakehouse and activate that data across the Google Cloud ecosystem. Roundel modernized its Target Product Ads technology stack from the ground up with borderless Lakehouse, completely rebuilding its data ingestion, processing, and measurement pipelines. If you are ready to get started with the transition to borderless Lakehouse for your organization, it doesn’t need to be difficult. For organizations currently using legacy Dataproc Metastore, we now offer an automated, zero-downtime migration path to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. This preserves your existing schemas and lineage while unlocking the AI-ready features of the borderless Lakehouse, so you can stop managing infrastructure and start activating agents. Get started today with the Build a borderless Lakehouse codelab or visit our website to learn more.

title: Modernizing perimeter security: Scalable perimeters with VPC Service Controls
raw_text: Agents represent a fundamental shift in cloud operations. They can act on behalf of users or autonomously, make non-deterministic decisions, and request data across projects at unprecedented speed and scale. Because agents are a distinct category of non-human identity (NHI), they require unique secure-by-default guardrails. Traditional, manually-operated network perimeters are vulnerable to today’s machine-speed attacks. Overly permissive perimeters, built to avoid blocked connections, increase the risk of unauthorized data theft, but overly strict perimeters stall development under a flood of access denials. Today, we're excited to announce key enhancements to VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) that make perimeters easier to create, maintain, and scale. You can now add folders to perimeter membership, so that projects contained in them inherit policy. You can also manage granular exceptions and resolve denials with guided, scoped remediation. The result is data protected by default, so you can scale autonomous agents across your enterprise without letting data leave your perimeter. This update is generally available, and at no additional cost. Perimeters aligned to your architecture VPC-SC provides a context-aware network security perimeter around your Google Cloud deployment, designed to secure your organization against data theft, even in the event of compromised credentials, identity and access management (IAM) misconfigurations, and insider threats. By extending network-layer protection across service-to-service interactions in Google Cloud's infrastructure, VPC-SC goes beyond traditional firewalls and creates an additional layer of defense that prevents access outside your corporate network — and is now easier for your organization to manage. Cloud administrators configuring VPC-SC can now include folders in perimeter membership , automatically extending the folder’s access policy to every project and nested subfolder it contains. New workloads can inherit protection by default, with no further modification. Figure 1: Simplified perimeter authoring in VPC-SC. Perimeter membership updates when a project is moved, simplifying lifecycle maintenance. Security coverage follows the resource hierarchy that your organization already governs, and compliance verification requires only confirming that the resource is located in the correct part of the hierarchy. Dry-run mode also supports folder membership, helping administrators evaluate the effect of a hierarchy-wide perimeter against live traffic before enforcement. Folder and organization support in ingress and egress rules Well-defined ingress and egress rules establish granular, context-aware perimeters without sacrificing operational flexibility across complex multi-project environments. Security administrators can now specify Google Cloud folders and organizations directly within those rules. A single hierarchy reference stands in for the set of projects beneath it, which keeps rules concise, keeps attribute counts well within quota limits, and extends access automatically to projects created later in the hierarchy. Figure 2 : Simplified authoring of ingress/egress rules. Using Private Service Connect endpoints in ingress and egress rules Enterprises increasingly use private paths to reach desired endpoints in their deployment instead of exposing the traffic to the internet. Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs are now supported as an attribute in ingress and egress rules. Administrators can author a rule that authorizes access specifically over a designated private endpoint, producing a policy that corresponds directly to the connectivity architecture it is intended to govern. Figure 3: Supporting Private Service Connect endpoints with ingress and egress rules. For organizations that have standardized on Private Service Connect, including endpoints propagated across the estate through Network Connectivity Center , this provides both a more precise and a more concise means of expressing source for the request. Service patterns in VPC accessible services Service patterns in VPC accessible services provide granular control over Google APIs accessed with private Virtual IP addresses (VIP), permitting interoperability beyond just VPC-SC integrated services. If the workload requires controlled access to validated API endpoints over a private path, administrators can now allow only the specific API URL patterns required. Additionally, the capability supports appending org-restriction-headers with egress requests to facilitate access to only authorized domains and resources. Because you don’t need to manage egress-proxy, you can accommodate legitimate operational requirements while maintaining a tightly-bounded private path, instead of choosing between a broad allowance and no access at all. Figure 4: Granular control over Google APIs with service patterns in VPC accessible services. Guided violation remediation VPC-SC perimeter policies evolve continuously alongside the workloads they protect, and administrators periodically need to authorize a legitimate access request not yet covered. New Guided Violation Remediation in VPC-SC Violation Analyzer cuts resolution time for blocked requests from days to minutes by generating a policy fix with remediation recommendations, which you can validate in Dry-Run mode first. Rather than just diagnosing why the violation occurred for a given denial, Violation Analyzer evaluates the blocked request against the applicable perimeter configuration, and proposes a specific configuration change, narrowly scoped by least-privilege design principles, to authorize the traffic: an ingress rule, an egress rule, an access level, or an update to VPC accessible services. This relieves pressure on administrators to broadly open up a perimeter just to resolve a violation and get an application working quickly. Read more about how BlackLine uses Violation Analyzer to streamline investigations . Figure 5 : VPC-SC Violation Remediation for faster turn-around. Get started today VPC-SC makes it simple and automated to deploy and refine granular network perimeter protection, even for autonomous agents. To get started: Establish your folder baseline : Identify the folders in your resource hierarchy that correspond to the boundaries you intend to enforce, and define perimeters around them so that new workloads inherit policy on creation. Run risk-free in Dry-Run mode : Observe production traffic safely without blocking active developers. Unblock traffic with Violation Analyzer and Violation Dashboard : Use automated least-privilege remediation recommendations to resolve any denials that surface. Enforce with confidence : Secure your full data estate by transitioning to enforcement once your dry-run logs show your intended access with clean, authorized traffic. To learn more about how VPC-SC can help simplify your data security posture and confidently secure your autonomous agent fleets, check out the VPC-SC documentation .
