title: Cyberattack AIs must be trained only on air-gapped systems, hundreds of AI researchers say
raw_text: Current security procedures for training AI models are inadequate, hundreds of AI researchers have warned governments and the AI community. They are calling for tougher rules and the establishment of a new international body overseeing best practice for AI development. In an open letter the AI specialists — 487, at time of publication, including many senior academics — called for more AI safety research and greater emphasis on containment technologies. “Strong sandboxing mechanisms including air-gapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” say the signatories, who include such luminaries as Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio. The experts said that a new international body, to be set up in consultation with governments and a wide range of AI and security specialists, could set new safety standards but also act as an organization to which containment failures could be reported, improving transparency for learning and accountability purposes. The scientists’ demands go further than some recent calls for greater regulation of AI. Earlier this week, Microsoft president Brad Smith said AI is less regulated than washing machines or milk, although he made no firm proposals to rectify the situation. And the UK parliament is looking at ways to improve AI security , although any moves will be hampered by disagreement among AI businesses. Hinton and Bengio are no strangers to this kind of scientist-led initiative. In October last year, they signed an open letter warning of the dangers of developing super-intelligent AI . The letter appears not to have affected AI’s breakneck development; it remains to be seen whether AI players in boardrooms will heed the warning.
summary: Current security procedures for training AI models are inadequate, hundreds of AI researchers have warned governments and the AI community. They are calling for tougher rules and the establishment of a new international body overseeing best practice for AI development. In an open letter the AI specialists — 487, at time of publication, including many senior academics — called for more AI safety research and greater emphasis on containment technologies. “Strong sandboxing mechanisms including air-gapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” say the signatories, who include such luminaries as Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio.

title: Malware evasion made easier with AI — but behavior still gives it away
raw_text: Fresh research suggests recent panic over AI-generated malware may be overblown. Last month Anthropic detailed how Russia-linked cyberespionage group Midnight Blizzard used Claude to rebuild malware each time security tools flagged its backdoor as malign. “We observed GTG-20006 operate through customized AI-driven workflows that automated much of their operations from development, infrastructure acquisition, phishing, persistence through command and control, to data exfiltration,” the AI company wrote in its report, referring to Midnight Blizzard, aka APT29 and Cozy Bear, as GTG-20006. While the group’s use of AI as part of its operations is notable, what raised eyebrows was how it did so as part of its evasion strategy: “If their monitoring AI agents identified that any of their deployed malware was detected by a security product, agents would then set about the process of autonomously modifying and rebuilding the malware to evade the existing detections. The agents were designed to continue iterating on GTG-20006’s toolkit until it was undetected,” Anthropic reported. That autonomous loop — from monitoring for detection to rebuilding the malware to fine-tune evasion — raises the spectre of polymorphic AI malware , malicious software that changes its code structure automatically while keeping the same core functionality. But threat intelligence company ReversingLabs (RL) has since released a report detailing how its telemetry and behavior-based threat hunting flagged the campaign’s Go backdoor PowerShell stager as malicious on Aug. 1, weeks before Anthropic’s Sept. 10 report. RL subsequently saw five versions of the same stager over the course of 25 days. Although each had a different hash, all five behaved the same way. That consistent behavior profile left each iteration open to detection, according to a technical blog post by ReversingLabs published last week, as analysts could still hunt for what the malware did and how its files and infrastructure were connected. As a result, evasion via AI rebuilds may not yet be as foolproof as first feared. Variations on a well-worn theme Changing a file to dodge detection is one of the oldest techniques in the business, and polymorphic malware has been deployed to dodge signatures for decades. “What stands out with this Midnight Blizzard activity is outsourcing the busywork to an LLM,” says Ben Bernstein, manager of the cybersecurity advisors team at managed detection and response firm Huntress. “They wired an AI agent to monitor security tools and automatically generate fresh variants without human intervention. We have seen basic script automation do this, but large language models just make the refactoring cleaner and faster.” Huntress backs ReversingLabs’ argument that while AI makes malware faster to rebuild it fails to change the hallmarks of its malicious behavior. “Models are fantastic at scrambling code structure and swapping variables to bypass static analysis,” says Bernstein. “But the AI is not inventing novel exploits. It just automates the grunt work of rewriting the same script to ensure the file hashes change.” In short, Bernstein says, “the packaging looks different, but the payload’s core objective remains exactly the same.” Malicious experiments in AI-assisted malware development Still, AI-assisted malware rebuilding is an emerging if not unprecedented tactic among malware developers. For example, Google documented PromptFlux in late 2025 , an experimental script that asked Gemini to rewrite its own source every hour, and PromptSteal, which APT28 used against Ukraine to generate commands at runtime. In March 2026, Microsoft released a report describing how the North Korean cluster Coral Sleet is using agentic AI tools to generate, test, and deploy payloads. “Most of these are early or experimental, and Microsoft’s own assessment is that the capability ‘remain[s] limited by reliability, latency, and operational risk,’” says Igor Lasic, SVP of engineering at ReversingLabs. But this most recent case involving Midnight Blizzard is the “clearest one on record,” according to Lasic, because two independent sources described the same infrastructure: Microsoft on July 31 as CaptiveCrunch , naming the files CornFlake and ChocoShell, and Anthropic on Sept. 10 with visibility into how the operator used Claude. “We held both files from July 6 and July 10, before either report,” says Lasic. Persistent limitations Still, ReversingLabs’ recent report may reflect only the current state of the art of AI-assisted malware rebuilding, as some of the limitations that characterized the Midnight Blizzard instance could be something more advanced models might overcome, Lasic concedes. “Today a model rewrites the file for free but cannot cheaply rewrite the server code that parses the beacon, re-register domains or re-phish victims, so the indicators that survived were the ones that had to change in two places at once,” Lasic explains. “A more capable agent with access to the whole operation could coordinate those changes, and I expect infrastructure indicators to age faster over the next few years, the way hashes already have.” While cost and the availability of more sophisticated models is perhaps only a temporary limit for AI-assisted malware rebuilding, two other limits are closer to fundamental: the behavior of malicious code and clues left behind during a malicious campaign that enable detection. “An implant that steals credentials has to read the credential store and one that calls home has to open a connection, whatever built it,” says Lasic. “Obfuscation makes that harder to extract, but no rewrite removes a requirement without removing the capability.” Furthermore, a model can change the next build but not the builds already observed, timestamped and linked to the same server. “Rebuilding faster produces more artefacts, and each one is another thread back to the operation,” Lasic concludes. Huntress’ Bernstein backs ReversingLabs assessment that behavior-based hunting will remain effective against even AI-assisted malware development. “You can disguise malicious code all day, but if a script tries to dump credentials or establish persistence, most modern EDRs [endpoint detection and response tools] will detect the action itself,” says Bernstein. Another limitation of AI-assisted malware development is that even the latest models are trained to abuse known security vulnerabilities. “They [AI models] remix known patterns rather than dreaming up zero-days,” Bernstein concludes. “Future models might get better if they can actively test their output against live environments to find undiscovered flaws, but for now, they are just recycling known techniques at a higher speed.”

title: No click required: How the ad industry became a pipeline for mercenary spyware
raw_text: That ad you just scrolled past on your phone but barely spared a look or click? It could be tracking your movements and collecting your data, without you having to do a thing. This “zero-click mercenary spyware,” dubbed “AdFection,” is increasingly exploiting a sprawling online advertising ecosystem ripe for abuse, according to researchers at The Citizen Lab . One top actor in the space, Discover-Tech, runs the Controlium platform that allows cyber criminals to “precisely profile and de-anonymize” millions of users, fingerprint them, and automatically infect their devices when an ad is displayed. Troublingly, Discover-Tech is successfully masquerading as a legitimate ad company across the online ad sales environment, the researchers said, listed as a “certified” and “approved” vendor by the likes of Google and IAB Europe. Over a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on nearly 200,000 unique websites and in Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Furthermore, its ads have been presented through major networks like Google, Yandex, and Beeswax, and it even exploited the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target victims in the EU. The Citizen Lab researchers disclosed their findings to Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi, all of whom took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem. “Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse,” the researchers warned. How AdFection exploits a largely unprotected system The online ad market operates largely via real-time bidding (RTB), auctions hosted by ad exchanges. Run by companies like Google, these take place “hundreds of billions” times a day, the researchers explained. When an ad box pops up on an app or website on a user’s device, it immediately triggers a bid request; advertisers then submit their offers, and the exchange grants a winner the ability to push their ad to the user within split seconds. These ads can contain images, video, and, most importantly to cybercriminals, code. Demand-side platforms (DSPs) and supply-side platforms (SSPs) act as intermediaries in the process, and data about specific users and devices is shared across the exchanges so advertisers can decide whether they want to show specific ads to a specific individual, based on device identifiers and characteristics such as a user’s precise location, cookie ID, mobile ad ID, or IP address. “The auction system is designed to enable targeting single individuals,” the researchers explained. “The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable.” Companies with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge, across cellular, Wi-Fi, and virtual private networks (VPNs). Discover-Tech has effectively infiltrated and connected the spyware industry to this online ecosystem, which includes infamous Israeli mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. Its partners can deliver ads to “mass-profile unwitting phone users,” and silently infect the devices of select targets, according to the researchers. When Discover-Tech wins a bid, one of its ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. Sometimes this is seen by the user; other times is merely renders in the background. Many of these ads have been shown to devices on national security-sensitive networks, in security organizations including NATO, networks associated with critical infrastructure, and media organizations around the world. Using AdFection, Candiru’s spyware infected devices at international news network Al Jazeera. The researchers emphasized that a Discover-Tech ad impression does not mean that a device has been infected with spyware. However, the fact that the company has been able to bid on and show ads across sprawling ad networks highlights a “systemic risk” warranting “urgent investigation.” Lack of vetting Discover-Tech’s ads carried no exploit at all, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “The ad was clean; that is the frightening part. Nobody clicked anything.” Instead, each ad called home with the device’s advertising ID and IP address. In almost every case, the server sent back nothing, Dickson emphasized; only chosen targets received malicious code. “Third-party verification scanners saw a harmless banner, because for nearly every viewer, it was one,” he said. This is exactly how tags slipped past verification. Also alarming is the reach: Discover-Tech’s ads displayed in 75,373 apps and 120,768 websites over the course of four months, and had impressions on networks belonging to NATO, Intel, Microsoft, and Apple. While the report emphasizes that an impression is not an infection, the company’s targeting clearly reached enterprise networks, Dickson said. Just as troublingly is the badge: Discover-Tech was listed as a certified or approved vendor for years. The report said that vetting often amounted to self-attestation, a box checked on a form. “A certification is only as good as the vetting behind it,” Dickson said. Steps enterprises should take now On managed browsers, ad blockers are necessary, but they’re not wholly sufficient, Dickson said. Many Discover-Tech bids were for ads inside mobile apps, typically overlooked by browser extensions. But clearly, desktops are at play too; Candiru targeted Al Jazeera’s Windows software. Dickson advised enterprises to: Push a vetted ad-blocking extension to managed browsers through policy rather than leaving it to users to install it. Favor browsers with built-in tracking protection. Block ad and tracking domains at the DNS or secure web gateway layer; this reaches in-app ads on managed phones. Disable advertising identifiers on corporate mobile devices through mobile device management (MDM) and restrict ad-supported consumer apps on devices holding sensitive data. Turn on Apple’s Lockdown Mode for high-risk executives, journalists, and any users traveling to sensitive locations. Keep browsers and operating systems patched “The ad is only the delivery truck; the exploit still needs a flaw,” he pointed out. Watch traffic tied to ad impressions for odd follow-on requests. Finally, search domain name system (DNS) and proxy logs for the domains published in the report. The advertising ID in particular deserves a hard look, Dickson pointed out. The Citizen Lab report says that blocking advertising identifiers alone would have stopped this attack method. Troublingly, he noted, many enterprises spend fortunes managing their users’ identities, then let corporate phones hand that persistent identifier to anonymous auctions that run hundreds of billions of times a day. “Every ad is someone else’s code running on your device,” Dickson said. “Treat the ad network like any other untrusted vendor.”
summary: That ad you just scrolled past on your phone but barely spared a look or click? It could be tracking your movements and collecting your data, without you having to do a thing. This “zero-click mercenary spyware,” dubbed “AdFection,” is increasingly exploiting a sprawling online advertising ecosystem ripe for abuse, according to researchers at The Citizen Lab . One top actor in the space, Discover-Tech, runs the Controlium platform that allows cyber criminals to “precisely profile and de-anonymize” millions of users, fingerprint them, and automatically infect their devices when an ad is displayed.

title: TypeSafe’s Jev ‘even more susceptible to attack’ than LLMs, says security vendor
raw_text: Although the Jev model rolled out last month by TypeSafe claims to have significant advantages over traditional LLMs, a security report published Wednesday argued that its streamlined approach makes it more vulnerable to some kinds of attack, compared to traditional LLMs. “In some cases, [Jev] is even more vulnerable to attacks, with both adversarial text attacks and prompt injection being able to disrupt the model’s outputs, resulting in incorrect and potentially devastating actions,” said the blog post from researchers at HiddenLayer . TypeSafe did not respond to multiple requests for comment. LLM, or something else? There seems to be debate about whether Jev is technically a large language model (LLM), with TypeSafe suggesting it is not, but HiddenLayer saying that it appears to be one. TypeSafe has even coined a name for the category: System One , which TypeSafe described as “a new class of frontier models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly.” Jev is the first—and thus far, only—named product categorized as System One. Jev is a streamlined model designed to function machine-to-machine. Its approach allows it to perform tasks faster and to use fewer tokens. But Kasimir Schulz , the director of security research at HiddenLayer, the blog’s co-author, said that the accelerated approach robs Jev of some of the checks and balances that exist in traditional LLMs. This means that Jev can fall for some attacker tricks that current LLMs typically detect and refuse, he said in an interview. Despite this, “Jev is great. You should use it. It has a lot faster response time,” he said, with the caveat “it doesn’t have all of the protections” seen in traditional LLMs, so some attacks on it succeed that should have failed. “ TokenBreak , for example, normally does not work with larger LLMs, but Jev is vulnerable to it out of the box,” Schulz said. Although simply inserting characters in front of important words, as in the original TokenBreak attack, did not yield much, HiddenLayer’s blog noted, “we did notice that increasing the number of perturbations and improving their targeting led to much higher attack success rates.” But although traditional LLMs are typically able to see through such attacks, it pointed out, “System One models appear to be vulnerable. As a result, this class of decoder should be treated with caution, given that they are susceptible to both autoregressive LLM attacks and text classifier attacks, providing potential adversaries with greater optionality.” The post cited some examples: “On a simulated checkout page, an attacker-controlled advertisement caused the browser agent to click away from the user’s purchase [and respond to the ad] despite instructions to treat page text as untrusted,” it said. “In a separate classification test, targeted TokenBreak-style changes lowered toxicity scores for prompts both models had initially flagged.” The post argued that multiple risks are therefore associated with Jev. “A browser agent may immediately click a selected element. A moderation system may allow an input whose toxicity score falls below a threshold. A routing system may send a request to a different tool or workflow. Each of these turns a model judgment into an operational decision, and therefore, risk,” the post said. “When evaluating System One models, test those decisions in the application where they will be used. Include untrusted webpages, misleading task-related text, and modified inputs that preserve their meaning while changing their form. Monitor the selected actions and scores and put independent checks around outcomes that matter. Keep in mind that, under the hood, these are still language models at heart.” Analysts agreed with both the report’s methodology and its technical conclusions, while also pointing out that a security vendor concluding that a new approach is not secure is somewhat self-serving. Philip Harris , an IDC research director, observed that the methodology described in the blog post “is sound, and consistent with established AI red-teaming practice: building a controlled test environment and probing for adversarial manipulation and injection is exactly the right approach.” But Gartner VP Analyst Nader Henein added that Jev, which was introduced on Sept. 15, is so new that he thinks some of the flaw reports were premature. “Jev will go through the same maturity process as do all other models, including susceptibility to seemingly rudimentary manipulation attempts,” Henein said. “This model was only released last month, so being surprised that it has issues is similar to being surprised when your baby drools.” However, Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, noted that the same attributes that make Jev so attractive also expose it to riskier behavior. “Jev can only choose from options the developer puts on the menu,” he said. “It limits attack paths. However, if ‘click any element on the page’ is on the menu, the attacker’s ad is on the menu. That is an architecture decision, and the buyer makes it.” He pointed out, “Jev makes AI decisions faster and cheaper, which also makes the wrong decisions faster and cheaper. Speed is a feature. It is not a security control.” Independent technology consultant Steven Eric Fisher agreed. “Constraining the format of a decision does not necessarily constrain the correctness, trustworthiness, or consequences of that decision,” he said, noting, “the simulated checkout scenario [in the post] illustrates how an agent can be redirected from an authorized task by information introduced through a less-trusted component of its operating environment. The fact that the agent was explicitly instructed not to trust page content, yet still responded to the malicious advertisement, is particularly relevant.” This article originally appeared on InfoWorld .
summary: Although the Jev model rolled out last month by TypeSafe claims to have significant advantages over traditional LLMs, a security report published Wednesday argued that its streamlined approach makes it more vulnerable to some kinds of attack, compared to traditional LLMs. “In some cases, [Jev] is even more vulnerable to attacks, with both adversarial text attacks and prompt injection being able to disrupt the model’s outputs, resulting in incorrect and potentially devastating actions,” said the blog post from researchers at HiddenLayer . TypeSafe did not respond to multiple requests for comment. LLM, or something else?

title: Cisco warns of actively exploited Secure Email Gateway flaw
raw_text: A critical vulnerability affecting Cisco’s Secure Email Gateway product is allowing attackers to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. In an advisory issued on Wednesday, the company urged customers to apply available fixes after confirming that the flaw is being exploited in the wild. The flaw affects the product’s Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature and stems from improper handling of email attachments when the File Reputation service is enabled. By sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment through a vulnerable appliance, an attacker can execute commands with root privileges. Cisco released software updates to address the flaw, but warns that there are no workarounds that address the vulnerability. Exploitation is subject to preconditions Tracked as CVE-2026-76519 , the vulnerability affects physical and virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances running vulnerable Cisco AsyncOS software, provided two conditions are met. The File Reputation service needs to be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version is earlier than 25.3.0.5525. The File Reputation service is part of Cisco AMP, which helps assess the reputation of files passing through the email gateway. In this case, improper handling of attachments creates an opportunity for an attacker to write arbitrary files to the underlying operating system. Successful exploitation can then lead to root-level command execution, potentially enabling further compromise of the appliance. Cisco warns that attackers who compromise an appliance could access private SSH keys used to authenticate between members of an appliance cluster, potentially allowing them to compromise other cluster members. Attackers with root access may also remove or conceal evidence of their activity. Cisco recommends checking the appliance’s system logs for indicators of compromise using the command grep “System Security” system_logs. However, a clean result should not replace broader investigation: the vendor advises administrators to cross-check external network and firewall logs for suspicious traffic, including unexpected uploads from affected appliances or downloads from malicious IP addresses. Patches are available, but incident response matters Cisco lists AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 as fixed releases for the corresponding software branches. Customers on AsyncOS 16.0 are advised to migrate to a fixed release. The vendor also said the fix is available through Content Scanner Tools version 25.3.0.5525 and later, and that updating the tools does not require a software upgrade or appliance restart. For potentially compromised virtual appliances, Cisco recommends preserving forensic evidence before rebuilding the system, deploying a clean virtual machine, rebuilding its configuration without importing previous configuration files, and renewing credentials and cryptographic materials. Organizations should also assess other appliances in the same cluster. The company said it has already deployed the fixed Content Scanner Tools package for its Secure Email Cloud Gateway environment . The advisory does not disclose the number of victims or identify the attackers behind the exploitation.
summary: A critical vulnerability affecting Cisco’s Secure Email Gateway product is allowing attackers to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. In an advisory issued on Wednesday, the company urged customers to apply available fixes after confirming that the flaw is being exploited in the wild. The flaw affects the product’s Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature and stems from improper handling of email attachments when the File Reputation service is enabled. By sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment through a vulnerable appliance, an attacker can execute commands with root privileges.

title: Attackers exploit Palo Alto PAN-OS flaw for root access as CISA orders three-day fix
raw_text: Attackers are exploiting a newly disclosed flaw in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software to run code with root privileges, and US federal agencies have been ordered to fix it and check for compromise by October 17. Palo Alto Networks disclosed the vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, in a security advisory published October 14. The flaw “enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall,” the advisory said. “Very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface,” the company said. It rated the flaw 8.6 on the CVSS 4.0 scale, which is high severity, and assigned it its highest urgency rating. The company classified it as CWE-94 , a code injection weakness. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-0322 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, citing evidence of active exploitation. Forensic triage required The catalog entry marks the flaw as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. The directive “establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied,” CISA said in its alert announcing the addition. The entry directs agencies to apply the vendor’s mitigations or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. It lists the flaw’s use in ransomware campaigns as unknown. Yih Khai Wong, senior research manager for security services at IDC Asia/Pacific, said security teams should trace who can reach the management interface from outside a trusted network and review admin login history for unusual activity. “They should also check firewall configurations for unexpected changes, since a compromised device can be quietly reconfigured to remain compromised,” he said. “Patching is only part of the response,” said Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer. He said teams should check Panorama and every managed firewall and preserve evidence before making changes. Affected products and fixes The vulnerability affects PAN-OS on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama, in both virtual and M-Series form, according to the advisory. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected. “No special configuration is required to be affected by this issue,” the advisory said. Palo Alto Networks has released fixed versions for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2, with hotfix releases listed for each maintenance line. The advisory gave an estimated release date of Oct. 15 for PAN-OS 11.2.16, the upgrade path for customers on 11.2.14 and 11.2.15. Customers on unsupported versions should move to a supported fixed release, the company advisory said. Wong said management access to any device still awaiting a fix should be locked down, or compensating controls should be applied on the device. How attackers get in The advisory does not say how attackers obtained that access, when exploitation began, or how many customers were affected. “The entry point probably isn’t the bug itself, but weak management-access hygiene,” Wong said. He cited admin credentials stolen through phishing or reuse, management interfaces left reachable from the internet, or an earlier compromise that gave an attacker valid logins. “Once they can execute code as root on a firewall, they have control over a device that enforces security across the network,” Dubey said. Palo Alto Networks said the flaw was discovered internally. No workarounds yet “No known workarounds exist for this issue,” the advisory said. Customers with a Threat Prevention subscription can enable Threat IDs 510046 and 510047, which the company said provide limited coverage and require SSL decryption. “Variations may exist that cannot currently be detected,” the advisory’s FAQ said. The company said risk “is highest when you allow access to the management interface from external IP addresses on the internet” and recommended restricting access to trusted internal IP addresses. Wong said the narrow gap is a warning because a jump box only limits or slows access and does not reduce the damage from an intruder holding valid credentials. “The real risks are credential security and detecting misuse after login, not simply restricting the front door,” he said. Wong said enterprises should ask vendors why management interfaces keep emerging as the weak point instead of being locked down by default, how they detect misuse of valid admin credentials, and how quickly patches reach every supported version. “Until every affected release is covered, production systems remain exposed,” he said. “If an attacker gains control of a firewall, organizations need a clear way to determine whether the device can still be trusted,” Dubey said. Palo Alto Networks did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
summary: Attackers are exploiting a newly disclosed flaw in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software to run code with root privileges, and US federal agencies have been ordered to fix it and check for compromise by October 17. Palo Alto Networks disclosed the vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, in a security advisory published October 14. The flaw “enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall,” the advisory said. “Very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface,” the company said.

title: Ransomware extortion gets personal as attackers target employees’ families
raw_text: Ransomware attackers are expanding their tactics beyond encrypting corporate systems and threatening to leak stolen data. They are increasingly using AI in attacks, exploiting organizations’ own AI systems and even using physical intimidation by threatening employees and their families to pressure companies into paying ransoms. The Semperis’ 2026 Ransomware Risk Report found that 84% of surveyed ransomware victims experienced attacks involving AI, while 87% reported attacks targeting identity infrastructure. It also highlighted that attackers are exploiting technology and extending pressure beyond corporate networks to the people connected to their targets. While 41% of respondents reported physical or psychological intimidation, 37% said employees’ friends or family members had been threatened. The survey in the first half of 2026 covered 1,200 IT and security professionals across nine countries, spanning eight sectors including finance, healthcare, manufacturing, critical infrastructure and government. Extortion is moving beyond corporate networks Ransomware initially relied on encrypting files and demanding payment for a decryption key. As organizations improve their ability to recover from ransomware attacks using backups and recovery systems, attackers increasingly adopt double extortion, combining encryption with data theft and threats to expose or sell stolen information. Now, they are adding personal intimidation to their tactics. These include threatening texts, letters or packages, threats against family members and friends, physical intrusion, abduction, bodily harm and stalking. The report found that 25% of respondents said employees or family members had been doxed (their identities were revealed online without their consent), while 23% reported swatting , where they were harassed by fabricated emergency reports resulted in law enforcement being dispatched to a victim’s location. About 25% reported that employees or their family members required medical or psychological treatment, while 24% said they had hired additional security. And around 14% were even forced to change jobs, office locations, or move to a new home. “Threats that target corporate employees beyond corporate borders are an unusual new phenomenon that distracts employees from being laser-focused while at work on the job at hand. Now you’re trying to figure out how to protect yourself and loved ones against a threat that has crossed the boundary from work to personal life,” Chris Inglis, former US national cyber director and Semperis Strategic Advisor, noted in the report. Despite the fact that an organization might agree to suffer financial losses and restore their servers while rejecting ransom, the threat to hurt one of their employees’ spouse or kid creates additional pressure to decision making due to the fact that it involves more people than just a business. “Attackers do this by trying to build up a picture of an employee’s personal life using the information that is already available or leaked somewhere else before. It can include public information posted on social media accounts, professional networks, data broker databases, previously leaked information, and even information available in the attacked company’s network. Artificial intelligence can help speed up the process of correlating this information and thus create a personalized threat for a person,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and CEO at Primus Partners. Exploiting enterprise AI As enterprises connect AI agents to corporate data, applications, and identity systems, these tools are becoming another potential attack surface. Semperis found that 44% of respondents experienced attacks involving the manipulation of their own AI agents or systems. Courtney Guss, Semperis AVP of Crisis Management, said that if a company is adopting AI agents, one should consider that at some point, those agents will try to compromise identity systems, even if that action isn’t meant to be malicious. She added, “AI agents typically try to accomplish their assigned tasks by any means they can. One way they can gain more ability to operate in the environment is by getting permissions to other systems. The fastest path to get those permissions is to compromise your identity system, which effectively puts the agent into ‘god mode,’ enabling it to grant itself whichever permissions it needs to accomplish its task. Unfortunately, the agent then becomes a ticking time bomb.” Dhar noted that AI can be used by attackers to speed up the processes of reconnaissance, personalize social engineering, and accelerate the processing of information. Besides, weakly secured AI agents are another entry point for hackers into systems. In most cases, AI serves as an accelerating tool but does not stand alone behind attacks. While organizations increase their capabilities for restoring encrypted data, attackers continue to become even more aggressive in exploiting weaknesses of people and organizations. Closing the security gaps The evolving threat landscape raises questions about whether existing security controls and incident response plans are equipped to handle attacks that exploit AI systems and extend to employees’ personal lives. Experts suggest CSOs should take care of identity security, test recovery and limited access to AI systems. They should ensure robust, phishing-proof two-factor authentication of privileged accounts, least privilege approach, safe backups of identity systems and testing restoration. “AI agents used by the organization should have clearly defined owners and limited permissions. They should have human approval for all high-priority actions. The organization should also minimize information retention and access to sensitive personal information of employees,” added Dhar. In case an employee’s family is attacked, they should have a confidential channel to report intimidation, while HR, legal, cybersecurity, and corporate security teams should know when and how to escalate cases to law enforcement. Even tabletop exercises should simulate scenarios involving compromised identity systems, threatened data leaks, and threats against employees’ families.
summary: Ransomware attackers are expanding their tactics beyond encrypting corporate systems and threatening to leak stolen data. They are increasingly using AI in attacks, exploiting organizations’ own AI systems and even using physical intimidation by threatening employees and their families to pressure companies into paying ransoms. The Semperis’ 2026 Ransomware Risk Report found that 84% of surveyed ransomware victims experienced attacks involving AI, while 87% reported attacks targeting identity infrastructure. It also highlighted that attackers are exploiting technology and extending pressure beyond corporate networks to the people connected to their targets.

title: FPT and its ilk offer an alternative to Indian offshorers
raw_text:
When it was announced that Wipro would exit India’s wonderfully named “Nifty 50” index of powerhouse stocks at the end of September 2026, it felt if not quite the end of an era, then a tapering off of what was once an uber-trend in the modern IT services sector.

Indian IT offshorers boomed through the enterprise resource planning (ERP) charge of the late 1990s as enterprises sought to protect against the looming fallout of the Y2K bug and join up what had been mismatched enterprise applications.

Bloomberg saw the Wipro episode as reflecting the “waning clout” of Indian giants, and it may be the case that India has been challenged by an increasingly saturated market. But the news may also have been reflective of a more slow-burning trend: the rise of other services firms worldwide with the skills, hunger and culture to address artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging opportunities with a strong value proposition. 

Keen viewers of World Cup football pitchside banners may have noted the presence of Argentina’s Globant, while there are also significant players operating globally with roots in Malaysia, China and the Philippines.

But perhaps the most interesting of the insurgents is FPT, the Vietnamese juggernaut that is carving more than a niche through outsourcing, software development and other adjacent opportunities in much the same way that the likes of Wipro, Tata, Infosys and others from India did all those years ago.

Star of Asia

Vietnam is the star turn of southeast Asia’s growth, growing at over 8%, faster even than fast-risers such as Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. The country is consistently ranked as the top regional outperformer by McKinsey. Growth in the region is powered by technology, with Vietnam aspiring to become a global top 25 economy by 2038, propelled by state-backed initiatives to weave a digital identity, banking and government services fabric, supported by ubiquitous mobile broadband.

The virtuous circle also includes robust foreign financial investment, helping to attract the likes of tech superpowers including Apple, Intel, Nvidia and Samsung. A healthy portion of those investments focus on research and development (R&D) and sophisticated low-level engineering activities such as semiconductor fabrication.

But the jewel in the crown of Vietnamese tech scene is indisputably FPT, a wide-ranging player in software development, outsourcing, digital transformation, telecoms and infrastructure. The company even has its own university campuses where legions of the country’s youth pursue digital dreams and from whom FPT can cherry-pick talent.

FPT has become increasingly hard to miss. Its logo has even been on the sleeves of Chelsea FC footballers, the London club with which it has an ongoing partnership for fan experience and other transformation projects. And outside the rarefied world of elite sport, FPT is making inroads in both the public and private sectors of the UK and other countries outside its homeland.

Dang Tran Phuong, FPT head of Europe and Middle East, who joined FPT in 2004 and has held management roles in FPT’s US market unit and across key accounts in aviation and logistics, said its ambitions are sky-high, and its plan is to replicate its formula from its native country. 

“We believe that the UK and other countries want similar things,” he said. “Value, time to market and new skills. We are an AI-first company and we are good at complex challenges that can serve the UK, such as quantum computing and building AI skills.”

“We are an AI-first company and we are good at complex challenges that can serve the UK, such as quantum computing and building AI skills.”

Dang Tran Phuong, FPT

By focusing on AI and other emerging technologies, Phuong believes FPT has the formula to succeed everywhere. The firm’s current strategy encompasses nearshoring opportunities that capitalise on Vietnam’s choice geographical location, but also extends to having a global reach.

Phuong noted that FPT now has 85,000 staff across 30 countries, and 1,100 customers. Overseas outsourcing deals are up about 30% year on year (YoY) and $10m-plus outsourcing contracts are becoming more common. FPT recorded almost $2.7bn in total revenue in 2025. 

AI, of course

Emblematic of the rapid change and pursuit of a market-altering inflexion point is AI, seen by FPT and Phuong as a way to fast-track its progress in a world seeking talent in the space. However, he added, software engineering, industrial transformation, computer visualisation and even drones are on its menu of offers.

More recently, FPT has extended its ecosystem and the company now has far-reaching connections to many of the core technology providers that are critical to Western ambitions, such as Salesforce, Palantir, AWS, OpenAI and Sitecore. 

Another key area is cyber security, where FPT recently inked a deal with OpenAI to proactively protect customers using AI frontier models and agentic adaptations to processes and workflows. Rather than using third-party alternatives, FPT uses Casan, its own five-stage transformation maturity framework that lets clients evolve from ‘curious’ to a sophisticated ‘native’ stage, via augmented, standard and automatic steps. 

Phuong said that Casan is augmented by FPT’s FleziPT AI ecosystem. The results, he says, will be demonstrable in terms of time to market and cost efficiencies, with 60% shaved off development schedules and 30% greater developer productivity. 

FPT is working with giants including Microsoft, Nvidia, SAP and Anthropic to make FleziPT a centrepiece of industrialising AI for enterprises. A July 2026 Forrester Consulting survey, From pilots to reusable platforms: a blueprint for scaling enterprise AI, suggested that only around a quarter of enterprises polled feel advanced in their AI efforts, and FPT believes a ladder approach is needed.

Is Vietnam in the right place at the right time?

With geopolitics fraught and enterprises seeking new sources of innovation as well as lower cost bases, FPT and Vietnam may be in the right place at the right time, just as India once was.

Jon Collins, an analyst at Inter Orbis, said: “I am a great believer in diminishing thresholds and how they either enable new tech platforms – which is how social media suddenly exploded –  or service models. 

“AI is rapidly changing business models around software and service provision, enabling faster-moving organisations anywhere in the world to become players in this ecosystem, where they might previously have been slowed by skills acquisition or other costs of entry. 

“India previously threw its weight into business and technology education to respond to the demand for lower-cost outsourced services, starting with call centres and quickly shifting to more advanced business process outsourcing. With AI including open models, other countries can follow a similar trajectory without requiring such a significant national investment.”

Clients like the speed of work, problem-solving mindset and access to rare skills. 

Ashkan Marandi, head of engineering and product development at Davies Insurance, said: “We partner with FPT because they can provide us with offshore capabilities and speed, and to be able to use the technical experience within the BFSI [banking, financial services and insurance] sector.”

IDC analyst Linus Lai believes FPT’s distinguishing characteristics cover both skills and products: “FPT stands out for combining three things few providers have at once: an owned talent engine through FPT University; platform-led delivery built on reusable IP and a ‘best-shore model’; and a full AI stack that now runs from GPU infrastructure in the AI factory to agentic platforms like IvyHub, where IDC positions them as a Leader in Asia/Pacific.  

“That combination has earned FPT the right to win on execution at scale, which they have done successfully in Japan (their cultural alignment is a big factor in this). The next question is whether FPT can win in more strategic, forward-looking guidance and industry thought leadership. And there is that opportunity to shift toward outcome-based pricing and expand the AI factory globally.”

Of course, FPT and Vietnam have a way to go before they can be compared with India’s remarkable advances on the IT stage. But that formula of combining Western-style ideas, such as Google-like learning campuses, and the hunger of an outsider could be an attractive proposition to many in the West.

title: CMA to decide Microsoft strategic market status by February 2027
raw_text:
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has proposed designating Microsoft as a strategic market status (SMS) firm in its business software ecosystem, and will open a consultation under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 before making a final decision in February 2027.

The CMA views Microsoft’s business software as spanning five digital activities: operating systems, productivity software, security software, server operating systems and relational database management systems such as SQL Server. The regulator said the products reach more than a million businesses and public sector organisations, with around 20 million monthly users in the UK.

Its provisional findings point to a strong position across each of those five areas, with switching barriers and commercial bundling and integration advantages that other software developers struggle to overcome. SMS designation does not assume wrongdoing, but it would give the CMA power to consider targeted conduct requirements or pro-competition interventions.

The regulator set out an indicative roadmap across four areas: cloud licensing, AI features in productivity software, communications and collaboration software such as Teams, and security software. It proposed to gather further evidence on whether customers can freely choose AI tools beyond Copilot, how Microsoft’s bundling of security products limits choice, and whether customers can choose which cloud runs their software licences.

The CMA has framed the timing around an AI inflection point, arguing that as generative and agentic AI spread across workplace tools, the market remains open but risks closing if Microsoft’s ecosystem does not interoperate smoothly with rival AI providers.

The designation test has three criteria, relating to a turnover threshold, substantially entrenched market power and a position of strategic significance in the specified digital activity. Designation itself changes nothing in the market, the regulator stressed, because it describes a position of market power rather than wrongdoing, with any intervention following separately.

The headline finding from its work, the CMA added, was that customers face challenges switching away from Microsoft or using alternative providers alongside Microsoft products, and that this limits the constraint rivals can exert across the ecosystem.

Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA, said: “Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers.”

Separately, the CMA updated on its engagement with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft in cloud outside the formal designation process. It said it had seen progress in which both companies had connected their datacentres with rivals, beginning with Google, removed data transfer fees for customers switching cloud providers, and introduced a mechanism for customers and competitors to request greater interoperability, alongside AI tools to automate switching.

The regulator said more remains to be done, and it had agreed with both companies to focus next on how identity and access management works across clouds and on ensuring portable cloud architectures can be deployed and migrated without unnecessary barriers. It will publish a further update in spring 2027, while keeping open the possibility of a full SMS investigation in cloud.

Microsoft has consistently contested the premises of the investigation, arguing that it operates in a “vigorously competitive” market and pointing to the availability within its ecosystem of Google Workspace, macOS, Linux, PostgreSQL and Okta as evidence of contestability. It also contends that AI is “dramatically lowering the barriers to building high-performing enterprise software”, and notes that its 34,000 UK partners contribute £38bn in revenue to the UK economy.

The informal cloud route has drawn scepticism too. In March, Mark Boost, chief executive of UK sovereign cloud provider Civo, warned that “voluntary arrangements made with parties outside of the SMS framework will not provide real impact”, while the CMA itself emphasised that designation assumes no wrongdoing and remains provisional pending consultation.

The proposal follows months of submissions that mostly urged intervention. More than 30 organisations called on the CMA to designate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem as SMS, and the Open Cloud Coalition has estimated that Microsoft’s licensing practices cost the UK public sector around £60m a year, and more than £300m over the course of a Parliament. 

The CMA noted that the public sector accounts for around 10% of UK cloud demand and has advised on procurement as part of a broader push to diversify supply.

A final decision is due by the February 2027 deadline, with a provisional decision expected partway through. For enterprise IT leaders, the consultation marks the point at which the regulator’s powers move from market analysis towards potentially binding remedies.

title: International finance body espouses ‘sound practices’ for AI adoption
raw_text:
Financial services institutions across the world are being encouraged by international financial services body the FSB to follow 12 guidelines when implementing artificial intelligence (AI).

The FSB, which monitors and makes recommendations about the global financial system, has produced what it describes as “12 sound practices” that financial institutions should consider when adopting AI.

“The 12 sound practices emphasise the importance of organisation-wide AI governance and highlight considerations for managing risks throughout the AI lifecycle,” said the FSB, which is chaired by Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey.

In its work, the FSB brings together national authorities responsible for financial stability, international financial institutions, regulators and supervisors, as well as committees of central bank experts. The FSB said that the guidelines seek to promote coordination, cooperation and information-sharing among financial institutions and across the international financial sector in relation to the rapid adoption of AI.

‘Sound’ advice

The 12 practices are in two groups, the first of which emphasises “the importance of organisation-wide AI governance as financial institutions adopt AI”.

It recommends board and senior management play a pivotal role in setting and overseeing alignment between AI adoption and business models, risk appetite and strategy; maintaining appropriate governance framework with well-defined roles and responsibilities; incorporating AI risks into the risk management framework and effective documentation of AI use; and undertaking continuous learning and adaptation.

The second group of practices set out “a comprehensive framework for managing risks throughout the AI lifecycle from AI development and deployment”.

It focuses on effective and systematic assessment of the materiality and risks associated with AI use cases at inception and thereafter; selection of appropriate AI technologies; appropriate data governance; explainability of various types of AI and consideration of compensating controls; evaluation of the performance of AI use cases; appropriate and effective human oversight; management of AI-related cyber and information and communication technology (ICT) risks; and management of risks from third-party AI dependencies.

“The sound practices serve as a practical toolkit that financial institutions can tailor to their specific context and risk profile and integrate into existing frameworks, including those for cyber and third-party risk,” said the FSB.

It said that as AI technologies and applications evolve, it will monitor developments and update the sound practices as necessary.

AI breaking new ground

Banks are using AI across their businesses to reduce human intervention, with the technology beginning to reach new areas of the business, way beyond simply automating laborious processes.

For example, AI agents could replace humans trading in financial markets in a few years, according to HSBC investment bank boss Michael Roberts.

The bank recently announced cuts to its human wealth managers with plans to replace them with AI – and traders could soon face the same prospect, with the combination of advances in AI, quantum computing and distributed ledger meaning they replace humans trading in financial markets, said Roberts.

Another area where AI will play an increasing role is in supporting investment bankers in deal making, according to Bahadir Yilmaz, chief analytics officer at ING.

“There are teams of 10-20 people working on a deal for many, many months. This starts with going to clients for early-stage meetings, and when you go to these meetings you have to be prepared. You probably saw a lot of Wall Street movies, and there, you see a lot of analysts working through the paperwork and creating folders. This is an iconic cliche scene, but that preparation can be done with AI today.”

summary:
Financial services institutions across the world are being encouraged by international financial services body the FSB to follow 12 guidelines when implementing artificial intelligence (AI).

The FSB, which monitors and makes recommendations about the global financial system, has produced what it describes as “12 sound practices” that financial institutions should consider when adopting AI.

“The 12 sound practices emphasise the importance of organisation-wide AI governance and highlight considerations for managing risks throughout the AI lifecycle,” said the FSB, which is chaired by Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey.

In its work, the FSB brings together national authorities responsible for financial stability, international financial institutions, regulators and supervisors, as well as committees of central bank experts. The FSB said that the guidelines seek to promote coordination, cooperation and information-sharing among financial institutions and across the international financial sector in relation to the rapid adoption of AI.

‘Sound’ advice

The 12 practices are in two groups, the first of which emphasises “the importance of organisation-wide AI governance as financial institutions adopt AI”.

It recommends board and senior management play a pivotal role in setting and overseeing alignment between AI adoption and business models, risk appetite and strategy; maintaining appropriate governance framework with well-defined roles and responsibilities; incorporating AI risks into the risk management framework and effective documentation of AI use; and undertaking continuous learning and adaptation.

The second group of practices set out “a comprehensive framework for managing risks throughout the AI lifecycle from AI development and deployment”.

It focuses on effective and systematic assessment of the materiality and risks associated with AI use cases at inception and thereafter; selection of appropriate AI technologies; appropriate data governance; explainability of various types of AI and consideration of compensating controls; evaluation of the performance of AI use cases; appropriate and effective human oversight; management of AI-related cyber and information and communication technology (ICT) risks; and management of risks from third-party AI dependencies.

“The sound practices serve as a practical toolkit that financial institutions can tailor to their specific context and risk profile and integrate into existing frameworks, including those for cyber and third-party risk,” said the FSB.

It said that as AI technologies and applications evolve, it will monitor developments and update the sound practices as necessary.

AI breaking new ground

Banks are using AI across their businesses to reduce human intervention, with the technology beginning to reach new areas of the business, way beyond simply automating laborious processes.

For example, AI agents could replace humans trading in financial markets in a few years, according to HSBC investment bank boss Michael Roberts.

The bank recently announced cuts to its human wealth managers with plans to replace them with AI – and traders could soon face the same prospect, with the combination of advances in AI, quantum computing and distributed ledger meaning they replace humans trading in financial markets, said Roberts.

Another area where AI will play an increasing role is in supporting investment bankers in deal making, according to Bahadir Yilmaz, chief analytics officer at ING.

“There are teams of 10-20 people working on a deal for many, many months. This starts with going to clients for early-stage meetings, and when you go to these meetings you have to be prepared. You probably saw a lot of Wall Street movies, and there, you see a lot of analysts working through the paperwork and creating folders.

title: London AI concentration could stunt UK growth
raw_text:
About 100,000 vacancies for artificial intelligence (AI) roles were posted across the UK in the past six months, up 51% from the previous period, according to an Accenture survey.

Accenture’s Tech Talent Tracker revealed that demand for AI skills increased the overall tech jobs market by 21%. But these roles are concentrated in London, which had six times as many AI-related job listings as Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle and Liverpool combined.

In the wider tech sector, the biggest increase in demand for tech skills was in Manchester (35%), reaching more than 30,000 roles, followed by Bristol (25%) and Birmingham (17%).

London, in comparison, saw in excess of 250,000 tech jobs listed, which was a 24% increase on the previous six-month period. About two-thirds of the UK’s tech talent works in London, which equates to roughly 1.75 million people. Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle and Liverpool collectively account for just 13%, the research found.

But the survey report warned that the concentration of skills in London could stunt UK growth in the future, particularly with the increased need for AI experts nationwide.

“London’s strength as a global technology hub is undoubtedly a success story and has helped establish the UK as a serious player in AI. But as organisations race to recruit the skills needed to realise value from AI, the concentration of AI jobs and talent in one place presents a longer-term challenge for the UK’s growth ambitions,” said Sam Holmes, talent reinvention lead at Accenture UK.

“AI is not just the preserve of technology companies based in the capital. Businesses across every sector and region of the UK will need AI skills to remain competitive and unlock new sources of productivity and growth,” added Holmes. “Creating more opportunities for people to develop these skills across the country will be essential if the UK is to realise the full potential of AI, ensuring its benefits are felt in every corner of the country.”

Developers still in demand

According to Accenture’s survey, jobs that support the take-up of AI are also seeing a bounce, with listings in engineering and DevOps up 11% to 100,000, data analytics jobs up 19% to about 90,000, and cyber security roles advertised rising by almost 20%.

“The findings indicate that AI is reshaping technology roles rather than reducing demand for them. As businesses move from AI experimentation to embedding it meaningfully into their operations, a combination of engineers and data expertise is becoming increasingly important in building and integrating the systems that underpin it,” said Accenture.

Organisations may also look to reskill experienced tech professionals to enable them to combine their know-how with AI skills, because a large portion of the AI skills base is people in the early stages of their careers. The survey found that 40% of professionals with AI skills have fewer than six years’ professional experience, with about a quarter with two years’ experience or less.

“The findings suggest organisations may increasingly look to build AI capabilities through training and reskilling from a broader base of technical expertise, alongside specialist hiring,” said Accenture.

Holmes echoed a claim made by Infosys chairman Nandan Nilekani at the recent Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, where he described fears that AI would take tech jobs as “hogwash”.

Holmes said: “As organisations become more mature in how they use AI, demand is growing for the engineers, developers and data specialists needed to deploy and scale it effectively.”

He added: “Far from reducing the need for talent, AI is increasing demand for a wider mix of technology skills. Competition for AI expertise is already intensifying, meaning organisations will need to invest in developing talent alongside recruiting it if they are to keep pace with demand.”

But Sam Kingston, CEO of software services company Zenitech and former UK head of EDS’s UK private sector business, said the argument “won’t hold”.

“I agree to a point, but then it will drop, and it won’t create jobs,” he said. “It will actually make people more efficient, and that then means that the speed of delivery is faster, and you’ll also use fewer people, senior and qualified people, to do that.”

Kingston said mid-level and junior-level workers will be hit in the beginning, as those in senior roles will be working alongside AI.

title: MoD’s new SIEM, analytics platform up and running
raw_text:
The UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) has successfully deployed an upgraded security information and event management (SIEM) and analytics platform for its Defence Cyber Operations (DCO) team.

The new service is being delivered by IT services house Centerprise, which is overseeing commercial delivery, support, enablement and governance, and Elastic, which will take on the core SIEM capabilities – with the intent of ensuring the MoD’s cyber operators can get up and running quickly and without fuss.

“DCO deserves a platform that can grow with the scale of the challenge. Together with Elastic, we are building that capability while ensuring the MoD has the support to use it effectively from day one,” said Centerprise director of defence and security, Mark Brady. “Our structured governance and enablement approach ensures the MoD achieves maximum value and long-term resilience from this platform.”

Faith Bateman, regional vice-president of public sector at Elastic, added: “The MoD’s continued investment in cyber defence reflects its commitment to staying ahead of an increasingly complex hybrid threat environment, where adversaries operate across cyber, information and physical domains simultaneously.

“Through our work with DCO and Centerprise, we are enabling analysts to maintain a common operational picture across the entire environment, centralising data to accelerate detection and mission response, and allowing analysts to focus on high-priority threats,” said Bateman.

Traditional SIEM not up to the job

The core challenge facing the MoD’s new partners arose from the fact that its globally distributed military and ancillary workforce demands its networks must not only be constantly available but able to handle large volumes of extremely sensitive traffic, often relating to intelligence or military operations

The MoD had found that more traditional SIEM platforms were unable to keep pace with the ever more sophisticated cyber threats faced by a department of its nature. Historically, this led to visibility gaps and rendered its incident responders slower and less effective. Lacking strong governance and enablement meant even more advanced tools could never live up to their potential.

According to Centerprise and Elastic, the new, refined programme equips DCO with a “defence-ready” SIEM capability that will deliver more unified visibility, streamlined operations, and faster incident detection and response.

Some of the system’s public features include expanded visibility across the MoD’s networks to let cyber operators spot and contain malicious activity before it becomes a problem, and easier to follow workflows to ensure cyber responders can work quicker and ensure incidents don’t disrupt core military missions.

Meanwhile, structured training and oversight will hopefully help the MoD ensure its new platform is able to adapt as the threat landscape continues to evolve

The system’s resilience is underpinned by a tiered support model via which Elastic will take responsibility for providing advanced technical expertise, while Centerprise looks after orchestration, escalation and governance.

Hybrid warfare

The MoD’s latest deployment comes amid a growing threat from hybrid cyber-kinetic military operations targeting European states, which some authorities believe is in danger of spilling over into open war, likely against Russia.

In such a scenario, the true threat to the UK’s security would likely come not as it did during the Second World War – from a Nazi ground invasion – but from the kind of tactics used in Ukraine, such as electronic warfare and cyber attacks on digital infrastructure and communications networks, food suppliers, government bodies and utilities.

In his annual speech assessing the threats facing the UK, delivered earlier this week, MI5 chief Ken McCallum spoke of a “generational shift” in national security and spoke of how artificial intelligence (AI) in particular is “supercharging the cyber security contest”.
